# The scenario

The Georgia Department of Community Supervision is considering a risk model to guide parole decisions. Every person released to parole would get a predicted probability of being **rearrested within three years**. The department has two proposed uses:

- **Use A:** people above a threshold get **more restrictive supervision** (more check-ins, electronic monitoring, faster revocation).
- **Use B:** people above a threshold get **priority for reentry services** (housing assistance, job placement, a case manager).

The department has promised that the model **will not use race**. You've been hired to build it and to tell them whether that promise means what they think it means.

**What you're turning in:** this rendered document, published in the `assignments/` folder of your portfolio.

**How this assignment works:** it has less scaffolding than earlier ones. The **Week 11 lab** (COMPAS) is your fully worked example: almost every step here has a matching step there. Where the NIJ data behaves differently from COMPAS, the instructions below tell you. Everywhere else, adapt the lab code yourself.

| A5 part | Week 11 lab step |
|---|---|
| 3.1 odds ratios | Step 3 |
| 4.1 predictions + confusion matrix | Steps 4–5 |
| 4.3 threshold sweep | Step 5 (`rates_at()`) |
| 4.4 ROC + AUC | Step 6 |
| 5.1–5.2 errors by race | Step 7 |
| 5.3 what carries race in | Step 8 |

Two differences from the lab: the outcome is called **`recid`** (not `p_hat`), and you **fit on `train` and evaluate on `test`**. In the lab we fit and scored on the same data. So every `predict()` in Parts 4 and 5 needs `newdata = test`.


# The data

The National Institute of Justice's **Recidivism Forecasting Challenge** data: 25,835 people released from Georgia prisons to parole supervision, 2013–2015. Download the CSV from Canvas, put it in your portfolio's `data/` folder, and rename it `nij_recidivism.csv`.

A few things to know before you start:

- **Race is recorded only as Black or white.** The data includes no one else.
- **Counts are top-coded:** "10 or more" prior felony arrests is stored as text. `parse_number()` turns it into 10, which undercounts people with many more.
- **`Residence_PUMA`** is not a census PUMA code. NIJ grouped Georgia's PUMAs into 25 areas and numbered them 1–25 to protect privacy. You can use it to group people by place, but you can't map it.
- **`Training_Sample`** is NIJ's own train/test split. Use it.

# Part 1: Load and clean


```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)


nij <- read_csv("/Users/chloealimurong/GitHub/MUSA-5080-portfolio/data/nij_recidivism.csv") %>%
  mutate(
    recid              = as.integer(Recidivism_Within_3years),
    male               = as.integer(Gender == "M"),
    age_group          = factor(Age_at_Release),
    prison_years       = factor(Prison_Years,
                                levels = c("Less than 1 year", "1-2 years",
                                           "Greater than 2 to 3 years",
                                           "More than 3 years")),
    prior_fel_arrests  = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Felony),
    prior_misd_arrests = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Misd),
    puma               = factor(Residence_PUMA)
  )

train <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 1)
test  <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 0)
```

**1.1**

```{r}
#| label: counting train and test recidivism
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| include: false
count(train)
count(test)
sum(train$Prison_Years=='More than 3 years', na.rm=TRUE)
sum(test$Prison_Years=='More than 3 years', na.rm=TRUE)
```

There are 18,028 observations in the training set and 7,807 in the test set. 58% of people in the training and 57% test set was rearrested within three years. This was calculated by extracting the total of people rearrested with more than 3 years ('Recidivism_Within_3years') from the total observations of each set, then dividing that number by the total which was roughly 0.58 for the training and 0.57 for the test (10,421 in the training set and 4,483 in the test set.)

**1.2** Look at `Gang_Affiliated`. How many values are missing, and who are they? (Hint: cross-tabulate it with `Gender`.) What would happen to your sample if you added this variable to a model without handling the missing values?

```{r}
#| label: counting missing values
#| echo: false
na_gang <- sum(is.na(nij$Gang_Affiliated))
na_gang_table <- nij %>%
  select('Gender', 'Gang_Affiliated')
f_gend <- sum(nij$Gender == 'F', na.rm=TRUE)
na_gang
f_gend
```

There are 3,167 missing values for 'Gang_Affiliated', they are the women in this dataset. If we added this variable to a model without handling the missing values, our model would be inherently biased towards the male subjects in our data.

**2.2** Pick one variable from the right-hand column and explain, in two sentences, why including it would make your model look better than it really is. 

*Your answer:* Variables like 'Recidivism_Arrest_Year3' would make our model's performance look better because if they have been arrested within 3 years again, then we would have the better probability of predicting recidivism within 3 years since there's already data on it. The problem in using variables to be recorded after our prediction and ones so close to our prediction, is that the outcomes we predict are modeled after ones that already happened. So we would get high numbers because those outcomes happened in our training and test sets but not when we test in real life.

# Part 3: Build a race-blind model

```{r}
#| label: base-model
#| echo: false
base_fit <- glm(recid ~ male + age_group + prison_years +
                  prior_fel_arrests + prior_misd_arrests,
                family = binomial,
                data = train)

summary(base_fit)
```

**3.1** Exponentiate the coefficients. Interpret the odds ratio for `prior_fel_arrests` in one sentence, using the word *odds* correctly.

```{r}
exp(coef(base_fit))
```

*Your answer:* For every one prior felony arrests, the odds of being arrested again within three years are 18% higher.

**3.2** Constant on the odds, not on the probability. Use `predict(..., type = "response")` with `newdata` to compute the predicted probability for two made-up people, then add one prior felony arrest to each:

- a man, age 23–27, 1–2 years in prison, 2 prior felony arrests, 1 misdemeanor arrest
- a man, age 48 or older, 1–2 years in prison, 2 prior felony arrests, 1 misdemeanor arrest

How much does one more arrest change each person's probability? Why are the two changes different?

```{r}
#| label: computing the predicted probability for two made-up people,a dding one prior felony arrest to each
#| echo: false
people <- tibble(
  male               = c(1, 1),
  age_group          = factor(c("23-27", "48 or older"), levels = levels(nij$age_group)),
  prison_years       = factor(c("1-2 years", "1-2 years"), levels = levels(nij$prison_years)),
  prior_fel_arrests  = c(2, 2),
  prior_misd_arrests = c(1, 1)
)

people_2 <- people %>% mutate(prior_fel_arrests = prior_fel_arrests + 1)

results <- tibble(
  age_group = people$age_group,
  before    = predict(base_fit, newdata = people,   type = "response"),
  after     = predict(base_fit, newdata = people_2, type = "response"),
  change    = after - before
)

results
```
Adding one more arrest increases both of their probabilities of being arrested again, 4% for the younger man, and 2% for the older man. The two changes are different because the older man's probability was already lower. 

**3.3** 

```{r}
#| label: my-model
train <- train %>%
  mutate(Dependents = replace_na(Dependents, 'None')) %>%
  mutate(Program_Attendances = replace_na(Program_Attendances, 'No attendances recorded'))

my_fit <- glm(recid ~ male + age_group + prison_years +
                  prior_fel_arrests + prior_misd_arrests + Education_Level + Dependents + Program_Attendances,
                family = binomial,
                data = train)

summary(my_fit)
```

I chose three predictors to add to my model; Education Level, Dependents and Program Attendances. Without too much of a relationship with the other predictors, I believe these will help improve my model in determining the likelihood of recidivism. I added them under a few assumptions. Those with more education are less likely to be arrested again as there are more programs in place in educational institutions to help those with mental health issues that contribute to crime. If a person has dependents like children or other family members, they would be less inclined to commit a crime again because being in prison would mean a prolonged time and support away from family. The more a person attends intervention/rehabilitation programs, the more they become inclined to commit crime again since there's a clear effort made towards improvement.

# Part 4: Choosing a threshold

**4.1** Add a column `p_hat` to `test` with predicted probabilities from `my_fit`, and a column `pred_50` that pred_50s anyone at or above 0.5. (Parts 5 and 6 use these column names.) Then make a confusion matrix and compute sensitivity and specificity.

```{r}
#| include: false
test <- test %>%
  mutate(p_hat = predict(my_fit, newdata = test, type="response"),
         pred_50 = as.integer(p_hat >= 0.5))

#table(predicted = test$pred_50, actual = test$p_hat)

test %>%
  summarize(
    sensitivity = sum(pred_50 == 1 & p_hat == 1) / sum(p_hat == 1),
    specificity = sum(pred_50 == 0 & p_hat == 0) / sum(p_hat == 0),
    accuracy    = mean(pred_50 == p_hat)
  )
```
